cues.text: A Noblewoman Drawn to Poverty
Born in Assisi on July 16, 1194, the eldest daughter of Count Favorino Scifi, a wealthy nobleman of ancient Roman descent, Clare grew up in privilege and comfort.
Her family possessed a large palace in Assisi and a castle on Mount Subasio's slopes, yet from earliest childhood, she showed unusual devotion to prayer and personal penance.
These practices seemed increasingly at odds with the future her rank and wealth would ordinarily have secured her.
Her own mother, Blessed Ortolana, had undertaken pilgrimages to Rome, Compostela, and even the Holy Land.
She would eventually join Clare's own community in widowhood — a household, it seems, already quietly oriented toward the renunciation Clare would one day embrace so completely.
A Night Flight to Poverty
In 1210, at sixteen, Clare heard Francis of Assisi preaching in the streets of her city and was profoundly moved by his radical embrace of Gospel poverty.
Over the following two years, she sought him out repeatedly for spiritual guidance.
On the night following Palm Sunday, 1212, at eighteen years old, she secretly left her father's house and made her way to the small chapel of the Portiuncula .

There, the friars received her by torchlight procession, and Francis himself cut off her hair and clothed her in a plain religious habit — a decisive, irreversible break with the wealthy, protected life her family had planned for her.
The First House of the Poor Clares
After a brief period sheltered among Benedictine nuns while Francis arranged a permanent home for her, Clare was established at the small chapel of San Damiano outside Assisi.
It was the very chapel Francis had once rebuilt with his own hands after hearing Christ speak to him from its crucifix.
Her own sister and other women drawn to the same radical vocation soon joined her, founding what would become the Order of Poor Ladies, known ever since as the Poor Clares .
Defending Absolute Poverty Against Well-Meaning Reform
Clare spent much of her forty-year tenure as abbess defending the community's commitment to owning absolutely nothing, even in common.
She often faced considerable ecclesiastical pressure, because the poverty was so complete that successive popes and cardinals repeatedly attempted to soften the rule.
These included the future Pope Gregory IX, acting out of genuine concern for the sisters' material security.
Clare resisted every such modification with quiet but unyielding determination.
Just two days before her death, Pope Innocent IV finally approved her own definitively written rule.

This made her the first woman in the whole history of the Church to author a monastic rule formally accepted by the papacy, preserving intact the absolute poverty she had insisted on for over four decades.
A Vision Beyond Her Sickbed
Confined to her bed by prolonged illness in her later years, Clare is remembered by tradition as having received a remarkable mystical grace one Christmas Eve.
She was too unwell to attend the community's liturgy and, unable to leave her room, reportedly beheld the entire Christmas Mass celebrated across town.

As though projected upon its wall, the Mass appeared from the Basilica of San Francesco—a vision that centuries later would earn her, somewhat playfully but not without genuine theological point, recognition as patroness of television.
Legacy
Clare died at San Damiano on August 11, 1253, and was canonized just two years later, in 1255.
The Poor Clares she founded spread rapidly across Europe even within her own lifetime, eventually numbering well over a hundred communities.
They remain today one of the most rigorously contemplative and materially poor religious orders in the entire Catholic Church.
They are a living testimony to Clare's own lifelong, uncompromising insistence that the poverty Francis had embraced belonged, in its fullest and most radical form, to women no less than to men.
